data.title: ‘Not If, but When,’ Says Top Investor About Microsoft Stock
data.description:
Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) stock has made an impressive recovery from its early summer lows and is now trading around $500, putting it fairly close to its previous record highs.

After facing negative sentiment regarding its AI positioning, the rebound reflects renewed confidence in the company’s cloud and AI prospects. Azure growth has been a major part of that recovery, while Microsoft’s broader software platform gives it multiple ways to benefit as businesses adopt AI agents and other advanced workloads.

The bigger question now is whether Microsoft is prepared to spend aggressively enough to meet future demand. According to investor JR Research, who ranks among the top 2% of investors on TipRanks, the answer appears to be yes. JR believes the company’s latest signals point to a much more bullish view of long-term compute requirements than investors might have expected.

JR points to a recent Bloomberg report that suggests Microsoft could roughly triple its total compute capacity, from about 12 gigawatts today to as much as 38 GW by 2032. That figure includes both Microsoft-owned and leased facilities, so it should not be interpreted as a direct forecast for capital expenditure. Still, JR sees it as an important indication that Microsoft expects demand for computing power to remain strong for years.

The shift is notable because Microsoft had previously appeared more cautious about adding capacity, particularly amid concerns that the AI infrastructure boom could eventually create excess supply. JR believes that stance is changing as monetization opportunities become clearer and capacity constraints remain an issue.

Copilot is one reason for that confidence. Usage appears to be stabilizing, giving Microsoft a stronger foundation for expanding consumption and pricing over time. That makes a larger infrastructure commitment easier to justify because the company has more visibility into how the additional capacity can generate revenue.

Azure is also becoming harder for investors to overlook. Microsoft has disclosed that the cloud business has surpassed a $100 billion annualized revenue run rate, up from roughly $75 billion a year earlier. JR sees the decision to highlight Azure separately as a sign that Microsoft is ready to put its cloud growth opportunity more firmly in the spotlight.

There are still risks to the investment case, however. A much larger compute buildout could weigh on free cash flow margins and keep pressure on Microsoft’s valuation until management provides more detail on the pace and economics of that spending. The company also remains heavily exposed to OpenAI, although its platform now supports around 11,000 models, giving it broader exposure across the AI ecosystem.

Even after the rally, JR believes the fundamental picture remains attractive. Microsoft trades at a little over 25 times forward earnings, below its roughly 30x average over the past five years. “The overall risk-reward remains favorable across its fundamentals, margins, visibility, and copilot adoption,” the 5-star analyst summed up. “It positions the stock well in the next pullback for investors who are looking to double down before the re-rating advances further.”

Accordingly, JR rates the stock a Buy. (To watch JR Research’s track record, click here)

data.title: Oracle vs. Adobe: One AI Software Stock Is a Buy, the Other Is Too Problematic, Says Goldman Sachs
data.description:
Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) and Adobe (NASDAQ:ADBE) are two software giants trying to adapt to the new AI-driven paradigm, but both face huge challenges as they invest heavily in AI while trying to protect their existing businesses and justify their valuations. Oracle is betting big on AI infrastructure and cloud, while Adobe is working to defend its creative software franchise as generative AI reshapes how users create and consume content.

Both have also seen their share prices contract in 2026 as investors mull over the difficulties the two face, from the huge cost of building out AI infrastructure to the threat that AI could disrupt their core businesses.

So, are these software stalwarts doomed or do these stocks offer excellent value at their currently depressed states?

Following the pair’s recent earnings, Goldman Sachs analyst Gabriela Borges has been assessing their prospects and finds that only one is currently worth investors’ attention.

For Oracle, Borges believes the latest quarter helped settle some of the concerns surrounding its huge AI infrastructure push. Revenue came in slightly ahead of expectations, while cloud infrastructure revenue jumped 121% year over year as new capacity came online. Oracle also delivered 850MW of capacity during the quarter and completed its planned $20 billion at-the-market share offering, removing an important funding concern.

The bigger questions, however, lie beyond the current fiscal year. Borges says investors still need a clearer picture of Oracle’s capital spending requirements in fiscal 2028, how much additional funding the company will need and when it can return to positive free cash flow. For the stock to perform from here, she believes Oracle must continue adding capacity while proving that this investment is translating into backlog, revenue and ultimately gross profit. The analyst expects the company’s October investor day to provide some much-needed detail on these issues.

All told, Borges expects Oracle to execute successfully. She maintained a Buy rating on the shares and raised the price target slightly from $239 to $240, implying the stock will gain 70% in the year ahead. (To watch Borges’s track record, click here)

Adobe’s results also offered some encouraging signs, particularly around user growth and engagement. Borges points to more than 1 billion monthly active users, with creative freemium users surpassing 100 million. Firefly’s annual recurring revenue also grew 40% quarter-over-quarter, while AI-related ARR passed $650 million, up 150% YoY.

The challenge for Adobe is turning that engagement into sustainable revenue growth. The company has deliberately prioritized expanding its free user base and attracting new customers over near-term monetization, meaning investors now need to see how effectively those users convert into paying customers. Borges also notes that the shift toward more flexible, monthly subscriptions is weighing on RPO (remaining performance obligations). On top of that, the arrival of new CEO Anil Chakravarthy following David Wadhwani’s departure adds another element of uncertainty as Adobe tries to balance AI innovation, user growth and monetization.

Put that altogether and the negatives outweigh the positives for Borges. She reiterated a Sell rating, backed by a $200 price target. That figure suggests the shares will slide by 23% over the coming months.

The Street also clearly distinguishes between the pair. Oracle claims a Strong Buy consensus rating, while its average price target of $251.52 implies shares will gain 78% in the year ahead. data.title: Nvidia and Micron: AI Slowdown Will Punish One AI Stock More Than the Other, Says Investor
data.description:
Calls to slow the pace of frontier AI development put the semiconductor sector back on edge on Monday. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei recently argued that the industry should “pace the frontier” to give companies more time for safety testing, oversight and governance, with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and other AI leaders generally supportive of the idea. The market reaction was immediate, with several semiconductor stocks selling off sharply as investors questioned whether slower model development could eventually mean less spending on AI infrastructure.

But slowing the development of ever-more-powerful models does not necessarily mean slowing AI infrastructure demand. The bigger shift may be from training the next frontier model toward running AI at enormous scale. As inference costs fall, companies can afford to use AI for more tasks, while agentic systems can generate huge numbers of tokens through repeated reasoning, planning and execution. That changes what matters in the semiconductor supply chain.

An investor with the moniker Summit Research (SR) argues that this distinction is particularly important when comparing Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) and Micron (NASDAQ:MU). Both benefit from AI spending, but their exposure is different, leaving Nvidia more vulnerable if the industry places less emphasis on rapid frontier upgrades.

Promotion

Discover why XOVR identified Kalshi as an attractive private investment opportunity.

For Nvidia, the problem is not that demand for compute disappears. Inference should remain a huge source of demand. The issue is that a slower frontier could reduce the urgency to buy Nvidia’s newest and most powerful accelerators. If AI labs take an extra year or two between major model advances, customers may have less reason to rush into each new generation of hardware.

That matters because Nvidia has built its business around a rapid upgrade cycle. Each generation promises substantial gains in performance and efficiency, allowing the company to sell customers more powerful systems and support premium pricing. If frontier progress slows, however, the monetization of that annual cadence could become less predictable. Customers may continue buying Nvidia hardware, but they could put greater emphasis on cost-effective inference rather than paying up for maximum performance.

There is also a potential margin issue. Nvidia has argued that technological leadership and major performance-per-dollar improvements are central to sustaining its gross margins. A shift toward cheaper, inference-focused systems could therefore create a less favourable product mix, particularly if customers become less willing to pay for the very latest hardware.

Micron has a different exposure. Its HBM is tied closely to Nvidia and other AI accelerators, so a slowdown in frontier upgrades would still create some risk. But Micron also supplies server DRAM and NAND storage, areas that can benefit directly from the sheer volume of AI workloads.

Agentic AI requires large amounts of memory and storage to handle expanding context windows, KV caches and persistent data. That means Micron can benefit even when the AI industry is running more workloads on existing or less cutting-edge accelerators. Its opportunity is therefore tied more closely to the number of tokens being processed than to how quickly the frontier model itself advances.

SR also points to a crucial supply constraint. Micron has indicated that its HBM capacity is already accounted for well into 2028, while conventional DRAM is also facing tight supply. If frontier demand softens, capacity could potentially be redirected toward other memory products needed for large-scale inference.

That gives Micron a wider cushion. Nvidia remains heavily exposed to the pace of its accelerator upgrade cycle, while Micron can participate across several layers of the AI memory hierarchy.

As such, SR has downgraded Nvidia’s rating to Hold (i.e., Neutral), while the investor maintained a Buy rating for Micron. (To watch Summit Research’s track record, click here)

On the other hand, the Street has a bullish stance for both names, giving the pair Strong Buy consensus ratings. At $324.30, NVDA’s average price target points toward 12-month returns of 54%. Micron’s average target stands at $1,563.93, a figure offering one-year upside of 69%. (See Nvidia stock forecast or Micron stock forecast)

data.title: The Space Race Is Heating Up — and One Analyst Says Buy These 2 Stocks
data.description:
Once upon a time, the ‘space race’ meant the grand strategic competition between the USA and the USSR to gain control of the heavens. The superpowers designed and built satellites, manned capsules, orbital spacecraft and long-endurance space stations, and NASA even sent the Apollo landers to put men on the Moon.

Today, the space race is heating up again, but in a very different way. Yes, the governments are still involved – NASA’s Artemis program is targeting the Moon, the Russians have a Soyuz escape ship docked at the International Space Station, and other powers such as the EU, China, and India have large-scale space programs. But the real difference – and a lot of the innovation – is coming from commercial players working alongside government space agencies.

This past summer, Elon Musk’s SpaceX went public, in Wall Street’s largest ever IPO. The company is pioneering reusable large rockets, and has already made history with privately launched and/or publicly funded missions of the Falcon 9 rocket and Crew Dragon capsule.

Promotion

Explore ASTX for 2X leverage on ASTS

SpaceX is only the largest of a growing cadre of private space launch companies, however. Smaller firms are sending up satellites, designing new rocket technologies, and generally shaking up the industry. As Berenberg analyst Michael Filatov said earlier this month, “Falling launch costs have enabled a rapidly growing investable universe in which we want to own the bottlenecks and differentiated downstream applications. The collapse in launch costs has driven the space economy past $500bn in 2025, and is on track to exceed $1trn by 2030. Near term, defence and sovereignty budgets provide de-risked demand while commercial markets scale, and we believe pricing power sits with the few proven high cadence launch providers, though longer term, value migrates downstream to applications that scale at little marginal cost. We favour vertically integrated launch and differentiated/sovereign constellation capability that cannot easily be replicated.”

Filatov goes on to recommend that investors buy two space stocks – companies that will benefit in a hotter space race. We’ve opened up the databanks at TipRanks to get a close look at them; here are the details, and Filatov’s comments.

Rocket Lab USA (RKLB)

Rocket Lab, the first stock on our list of Berenberg picks, is a ~$37.5 billion space launch firm, with a proven, reusable, small-payload rocket available for customers, a deep work backlog, and a leading position among commercial launch firms in the low Earth orbit (LEO) niche. The company specializes, for now, in deploying reusable launch vehicles to send small payloads into orbit – a key capability, as it helps to populate the growing satellite constellations that are circling our globe.

Like any successful company, Rocket Lab has built its business around the needs of its customer base. It provides vital launch services for companies in such fields as satcom, communications, and imaging, and has also become an important contractor for various government agencies. All of these customers have their own idiosyncratic needs – but Rocket Lab’s rocket tech can facilitate their disparate payloads.

The company’s main tool right now is the Electron rocket, one of the space industry’s most-used launch vehicles in the US market. The Electron, which can loft a payload up to 300 kilograms, has made 95 launches to date, including 16 in 2026. Rocket Lab operates 3 launch pads, and boasts that Electron’s flights have put over 265 satellites safely into orbit.

Rocket Lab’s other vehicles include a test bed project, dubbed HASTE, for Hypersonic Accelerator Suborbital Test Electron. HASTE is designed to test suborbital, high-speed systems, and can carry a 700 kilogram payload. The company has another project in late-stage development, the Neutron rocket, which is designed to loft large-scale payloads, up to 13,000 kilograms, into low Earth orbit. The rocket’s specs even include an interplanetary launch capability, for sending 1,500 kilogram payloads to Mars or Venus. We should note, however, that Rocket Lab has recently pushed back the planned first launch of the Neutron; where it had been planned for later this year, the company now says that the first Neutron will be delivered to the launch pad during 4Q26, with the launch set for early next year. Like Electron, Neutron is designed to be a reusable vehicle.

Also of note for Rocket Lab, the company reported a record-level work backlog at the end of 2Q26 – totaling $2.36 billion and up 137% year-over-year. This is a clear indication of both Rocket Lab’s solid work offerings and the general expansion of the private space launch industry.

In that Q2 report, Rocket Lab’s revenue was also reported as a record – and at $234 million, the top line was up 62% year-over-year and beat the forecast by over $3 million. At the bottom line, Rocket Lab is running a net loss – not uncommon with leading-edge tech-related companies – but the GAAP EPS of ($0.08) represented an improvement over the 13-cent per share loss reported in 2Q25. The 2Q26 bottom line was in line with expectations.

Analyst Filatov, in his write-up here for Berenberg, notes that Rocket Lab has a strong business model, a sizable backlog to fall back on, and a quality catalyst in the near future. He writes, “We view vertical integration across launch, manufacturing and applications as the most valuable combination in space, carrying optionality not reflected in the headline multiple. With launch a clear industry bottleneck visible in preflight Neutron dedicated bookings and Electron backlog, upside to space systems estimates from the programme pipeline, a broad range of growth avenues in applications and a founder-led team that has repeatedly proven its ability to execute and expand its addressable market, we believe Rocket Lab is perhaps the most compelling and differentiated long-term asset to own in the space sector, particularly as its closest public peer, SpaceX, increasingly aligns itself with the AI theme. We acknowledge the execution risk and extreme multiple and would buy/add on volatility.”

The Berenberg expert’s take on Rocket Lab is clearly bullish, and his comments back up the Buy rating, while the $83 price target implies a one-year upside potential for the stock of 33%. (To watch Filatov’s track record, click here.)

RKLB shares have a Strong Buy consensus rating from the Street, based on 17 recent reviews that include 14 Buys to 3 Holds. The stock is priced at $62.55, and its $110.13 average target price indicates an even more bullish upside than Filatov suggests, at 76%. (See RKLB stock forecast.)

The company’s latest results reinforced that optimism, with strong growth in data center revenue, improving margins and continued demand for both its server CPUs and AI accelerators.

However, the problem for AMD stock is no longer whether the business is performing well. It is whether the company can continue exceeding the very high expectations already reflected in its share price.

Investor Konstantinos Kosmidis believes the long-term bull case remains intact, but argues that AMD is unlikely to receive another major valuation boost in the near term without a significant upside surprise.

That does not make Konstantinos bearish. AMD also expects the server CPU market to reach around $220 billion by 2030, while its broader addressable market could reach between $2 trillion and 3 trillion.

For the investor, the key distinction is therefore between a strong business and an attractive entry point. AMD’s fundamentals continue to support the bull case, but the stock now needs further evidence of upside to justify another significant rerating.

data.title: ‘Beware the Trap,’ Says Investor About Oracle Stock
data.description:
Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) is spending heavily to establish itself as a major player in AI infrastructure, but its latest results raise questions about whether that investment is translating into enough underlying growth. While its cloud business is expanding rapidly, other parts of the company are shrinking, creating a much less impressive picture beneath the headline AI numbers.

The key question for investors is whether Oracle is building a highly profitable AI business or committing enormous amounts of capital to an infrastructure boom that could eventually produce excess capacity and weaker returns.

Investor Elina Selianska takes a bearish view of Oracle’s current strategy. She argues that the company’s latest results deserve much closer scrutiny, particularly given the enormous amount being spent on data centers and AI infrastructure.

Promotion

ORCZ: built for a short position on ORCL

Selianska points out that Oracle’s total revenue barely increased sequentially, rising from $19.18 billion in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026 to $19.35 billion in the first quarter of fiscal 2027. That was despite $28 billion in capital expenditures during the quarter. Cloud infrastructure revenue rose by $1.6 billion, from $5.8 billion to $7.4 billion, but that growth was partly offset by a $1.27 billion decline in traditional software and support revenue. In her view, Oracle is effectively shifting revenue from its legacy business into cloud infrastructure rather than generating as much new demand as the headline cloud growth suggests.

The investor is also concerned about margins. Oracle’s traditional software business was highly profitable because its products had minimal marginal costs. AI infrastructure is very different. Data centers, GPUs and other equipment require substantial upfront investment, while depreciation begins once those assets are put into service. Revenue, meanwhile, is generated over time as customers use the available computing capacity. Selianska believes this shift could put sustained pressure on profitability.

Oracle’s balance sheet is stronger than that of some newer AI infrastructure companies, but the investor argues that shareholders are still bearing much of the cost. The company has around $117 billion of debt and faces roughly $1.4 billion in quarterly interest expense, while capital expenditure is expected to reach $90 billion to $95 billion for the full fiscal year. A $20 billion share offering has also helped finance the investment, resulting in dilution for existing shareholders.

Selianska’s biggest concern is the possibility of an AI infrastructure “supply glut.” Chipmakers such as Nvidia and TSMC are expanding production while each new generation of hardware delivers substantially more computing power. If supply of computing capacity eventually grows faster than demand, cloud prices could fall, leaving Oracle with expensive infrastructure that generates lower returns.

The investor acknowledges that sustained AI demand could allow Oracle to earn attractive returns on today’s investments. However, she questions whether demand can remain strong enough for long enough to absorb the enormous amount of computing capacity being built.

“Ultimately,” Selianska summed up, “cash flow is currently burned by capex, and future profits will be crushed by an overabundance of capacity. I think the company will transform from a high-margin software vendor into a low-margin, capital-intensive utility provider. They are building furiously, but they are building a trap.”

To this end, Selianska rates ORCL stock a Sell. (To watch Selianska’s track record, click here)

data.title: Broadcom vs. Micron: One AI Stock Has the Upper Hand, Says Investor
data.description:
The latest headlines calling for a slowdown in AI development might have spooked investors on Monday, but Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) and Micron (NASDAQ:MU) continue to benefit from the huge investment in AI infrastructure.

However, the two companies play very different roles in that ecosystem. Broadcom combines semiconductors with infrastructure software and has become a major player in networking and custom AI chips. Micron, meanwhile, is more directly focused on memory and storage, including DRAM and NAND, which are critical to the performance of AI data centers.

That makes the comparison less straightforward than simply looking at which company is growing faster. Broadcom offers broader exposure to AI infrastructure and custom accelerators, while Micron gives investors a more concentrated bet on the memory market and continued data center demand.

Investor Sara Appino, who contributes to The Motley Fool, has been assessing both companies to determine which one offers the more attractive opportunity for investors today.

Looking at Broadcom, the chip giant has secured significant commitments from companies including Samsung and Apple, and counts Alphabet as a major customer, although this comes with a notable drawback: customer concentration. Distributors account for almost 48% of revenue, while its five largest end customers contribute around 40%.

The financial performance, however, remains impressive. In its annual report for fiscal 2025, Broadcom generated almost $63.9 billion in revenue, up about 24% year-over-year, while net income reached roughly $23.1 billion. Its net margin was approximately 36%. More recently, the company reported third-quarter fiscal 2026 revenue of $29.6 billion, up 86% YoY, while AI semiconductor revenue jumped 221% to $16.7 billion.

Micron is much more concentrated on memory and storage, with around half of its revenue coming from data-center customers. That exposure has helped fuel a dramatic boost. Fiscal 2025 revenue climbed almost 49% to approximately $37.4 billion, while net income reached about $8.5 billion. More recently, the company reported record third-quarter fiscal 2026 revenue of $41.46 billion, compared with $9.30 billion a year earlier, while GAAP net income surged to $28.24 billion. Micron also guided for fourth-quarter revenue of approximately $50 billion.

Micron’s balance sheet is particularly strong, with a debt-to-equity ratio of around 0.06x and a current ratio of roughly 3.4x. But Micron also faces significant customer concentration, with more than half of its revenue coming from its ten largest customers. That leaves it exposed to changes in spending by major cloud and hyperscale customers.

Both companies face meaningful risks. Broadcom is exposed to hyperscaler spending, relies on TSMC for wafer production and faces legal and regulatory issues. Its AI opportunity is also tied to a highly cyclical semiconductor industry.

Micron faces its own challenges, including geopolitical restrictions in China, legal disputes, the technical difficulty of producing advanced HBM memory and the enormous capital expenditure required to expand manufacturing capacity, not to mention the cyclical nature of the memory industry.

From a valuation perspective, Micron looks considerably cheaper on measures such as forward P/E and price-to-sales. Broadcom commands a premium, reflecting its broader business and stronger profitability.

Appino nevertheless puts greater weight on Broadcom’s AI opportunity. The investor points to its rapidly expanding custom AI accelerator business and the unusually strong visibility created by supply commitments. Broadcom has a long-standing partnership with Google to develop and supply its custom TPUs, while also working with other major AI players including OpenAI, Meta and Anthropic.

Micron is also producing exceptional results, with record revenue, strong earnings and long-term customer agreements designed to provide greater pricing and volume stability.

But Appino sees memory as inherently more cyclical than Broadcom’s deeply embedded custom-chip relationships. “For a long-term investor, Broadcom’s locked-in AI revenue roadmap and operating margins that keep expanding make it the more durable foundation,” the investor summed up. data.title: Micron vs. Sandisk: The Opportunity Tilts in Favor of One AI Memory Stock, Says Investor
data.description:
Micron (NASDAQ:MU) and Sandisk (NASDAQ:SNDK) are two names that have drawn a massive amount of investor attention over the past year. Both have benefited from the surge in AI-related memory demand, but they offer investors different exposure to the market. Micron is benefiting from tight DRAM supply and strong demand for high-bandwidth memory (HBM), while Sandisk is more exposed to NAND and the outlook for flash memory.

That makes the comparison more interesting than simply looking at which company is producing the strongest results today. Both are trying to make their businesses less vulnerable to the sharp boom-and-bust cycles that have historically defined the memory industry. Long-term customer contracts are playing an important role in that effort, but the underlying supply outlook for DRAM and NAND could ultimately matter just as much.

Looking at both companies’ prospects, an investor using the pseudonym Delta Analyst (DA) believes Sandisk has made more progress on the contractual side. Its New Business Model agreements cover around half of FY2027 bits and two-thirds of FY2028 bits. The agreements generally run for more than four years and include pricing mechanisms designed to provide protection if NAND prices weaken.

Promotion

Micron has taken a similar approach with its Strategic Customer Agreements, although coverage is currently lower. The agreements cover around 20% of DRAM volume and one-third of NAND volume, with many contracts extending through 2030. They include take-or-pay commitments as well as price floors and ceilings.

So Sandisk has the more extensive contractual protection. But contracts don’t tell the whole story.

The bigger question is what happens to supply. DRAM is expected to remain tight through 2027 as HBM takes up a growing share of manufacturing capacity. HBM requires more wafer capacity to produce comparatively fewer bits, essentially putting pressure on the amount of capacity available for conventional DRAM.

NAND faces a different outlook. Manufacturing improvements, process migrations and additional capacity could result in looser supply conditions during the second half of 2027. That creates a potentially important difference between the two companies.

There are, however, some factors that could ease the tight DRAM supply outlook. Samsung, SK hynix and Micron could redirect more wafer capacity toward conventional DRAM if it becomes more profitable than HBM. China’s CXMT is another potential threat. The company is expanding DRAM production and has begun producing HBM3E in small quantities.

The investor does not regard CXMT as an immediate equivalent to the established HBM players, but its progress could become more significant from 2028 onward. If CXMT expands conventional DRAM capacity while successfully scaling HBM3E, it could put pressure on the industry’s current supply discipline.

Sandisk also has an advantage when it comes to cash generation. Its recent free cash flow represented around 56% of revenue, compared with roughly 44% for Micron. Micron is also heading into a period of much heavier capital spending as it expands manufacturing capacity.

DA therefore sees two different strengths. Sandisk has built a stronger contractual defence against the next memory downturn, while Micron has greater exposure to the part of the market where supply is expected to remain tight for longer.

After weighing those factors, Delta Analyst rates Micron a Buy and Sandisk a Hold, preferring the former over the next 12 to 18 months. The investor believes the combination of DRAM tightness, strong HBM demand, growing contractual revenue and substantial earnings power gives Micron the better opportunity. (To watch Delta Analyst’s track record, click here)

That preference is not without caveats, however. DA is deliberately assuming that today’s exceptional margins will fall as supply responds. CXMT’s expansion, changes in wafer allocation and the eventual normalization of memory supply could all weaken Micron’s advantage. Sandisk could also surprise on the upside if its contracts prove capable of protecting margins even after NAND conditions loosen.

For now, though, the investor sees Micron as offering the better combination of memory-market exposure, earnings durability and potential upside.

Wall Street’s stock experts see no reason to choose between the pair, with the analyst consensus rating both stocks as Strong Buys. Micron is expected to gain 60% over the next year, given the average price target clocks in at $1,563.93. Sandisk’s average target stands at $2,145, pointing to 12-month returns of 31%. But perhaps the biggest obstacle is trust. Helfstein argues that Muse will need access to users’ passwords to handle tasks such as e-commerce and other online services effectively. Yet Oppenheimer’s survey of 1,500 U.S. consumers suggests many people are not comfortable giving Meta that level of access.

Only 13% of respondents said they would share all their passwords with an AI agent, while 28% would consider doing so depending on the provider and 58% would refuse. Meta also ranked poorly on the question of which platforms consumers would trust with their passwords. Google scored 30%, Apple 23% and ChatGPT 16%, compared with just 8% for Meta.

Helfstein also points to relatively low consumer awareness of AI agents. While 41% of respondents had heard of them, they did not fully understand their capabilities, and only 10% had actually used one. Just 19% said they would pay for an agentic assistant, while 44% said they would not.

Finally, Helfstein sees a potential challenge from Apple. Google is expected to provide additional computing capacity for Apple Intelligence and Siri through Gemini, potentially giving Apple users a more capable AI assistant. With Apple and Google also enjoying greater consumer trust, Meta could have a tough time turning Muse into a major paid business.

data.title: ‘It’s an Outdated Trap,’ Says Top Investor About Micron Stock
data.description:
Micron (NASDAQ:MU) currently finds itself in an unusual position: record profits would normally be a warning sign for a memory stock, but this time they could be part of the bull case. The company is benefiting from an extraordinary shortage of memory chips as AI data centers consume supply faster than the industry can replace it. Micron’s latest results showed just how powerful the boom has become, with record revenue and profitability as demand continues to outstrip supply.

However, there is a catch. Memory is a notoriously cyclical business, and history suggests that exceptionally high margins can eventually be followed by falling prices, weaker profits and a painful downturn.

That raises an important question for investors: is Micron approaching the top of another memory cycle, or is AI changing the cycle altogether?

Promotion

Top investor Keithen Drury, who contributes to the Motley Fool and ranks among the top 3% of investors on TipRanks, believes investors shouldn’t assume that history will simply repeat itself.

The memory industry is cyclical largely because its products are commoditized. Micron competes with Samsung and SK hynix, and customers can move between suppliers when they can get a better price. That makes supply and demand critical to the industry’s profitability.

At the moment, though, demand is unlike anything Micron has seen before. Hyperscalers are spending huge sums on AI data centers, and those facilities require enormous amounts of memory. Demand has grown faster than Micron and its competitors can add production, creating a shortage that has pushed memory prices sharply higher. Micron itself says AI-driven demand is growing faster than the industry’s ability to increase supply.

That has translated into extraordinary margins. And this is where the historical argument becomes important. Over the past two decades, Micron’s profitability has moved dramatically with the memory cycle. The company experienced major downturns during the 2008-09 financial crisis and again in 2023. Even the previous major peak was followed by a substantial decline. Before reaching its current margin peak, Micron’s profitability previously peaked in fiscal Q4 2018, when gross margin reached 61% and operating margin hit 51.9%.

The obvious concern is that the current boom could eventually produce the same result. If new fabs bring enough capacity online, supply could catch up with demand. Memory prices could then fall, taking Micron’s margins and earnings with them.

Drury’s argument is that the timing could be very different this time.

Micron’s management expects the current supply tightness to persist beyond 2027, giving the company a longer period of unusually strong demand. And while additional capacity should eventually ease the shortage, that doesn’t necessarily mean the AI spending boom will end. The broader build-out of AI infrastructure is expected to continue for years, potentially keeping demand elevated even after the current supply crunch fades.

There is another important difference. Micron has signed multiyear strategic agreements with major customers that include committed volumes and pricing protections. The company says these contracts provide greater visibility and stability and could make its financial performance more predictable than in previous cycles.

That doesn’t mean Micron’s margins can stay at record levels forever. Drury expects profitability to normalize eventually. But if AI keeps demand strong through the end of the decade, Micron could remain highly profitable even after the current shortage ends. “I don’t think history will repeat itself for Micron’s stock through 2030, and that makes it a strong buy now,” the 5-star investor summed up. data.title: WDC, STX and SNDK: Which AI Storage Stock Is the Most Appealing Right Now? Top Investor Weighs In
data.description:
The AI revolution is driving a major expansion in data center capacity, and that is translating into unusually strong demand for storage.

Western Digital (NASDAQ:WDC), Seagate Technology (NASDAQ:STX) and Sandisk (NASDAQ:SNDK) are all seeing customers commit to storage capacity well in advance, giving the companies much better visibility into future demand than they typically have. But while all three are benefiting from the same trend, the deals they have secured offer different levels of protection, particularly when it comes to pricing.

Investor David Sparks, who contributes to The Motley Fool and ranks among the top 1% of investors on TipRanks, has compared the three stocks, focusing on how much future business is already secured and how much confidence investors can have in the earnings ahead.

Western Digital has plenty of momentum. The company generated $3.75 billion in fiscal fourth-quarter revenue, a 44% increase from a year earlier, while adjusted gross margin climbed to 54.4% and EPS more than doubled. Its customer base has also become heavily concentrated in the cloud, which accounted for 89% of revenue in the fiscal third quarter.

Sparks sees a potential weakness, however. Western Digital has secured major orders for 2026 and has longer-term arrangements with some of its biggest customers, but investors don’t have a clear picture of how much production is covered beyond the current year. If the storage market eventually turns lower, that could leave the company exposed when today’s agreements expire.

The valuation isn’t particularly demanding at around 14 times expected fiscal 2028 earnings. Sparks therefore sees enough to keep the stock interesting, but not enough contractual visibility to make it his preferred choice.

Seagate has given customers more certainty over both demand and pricing. The company says its build-to-order arrangements already establish the products customers will receive and the prices they will pay throughout calendar 2027. It has also allocated most of its nearline capacity, which is widely used by cloud data centers, through 2028.

The financial numbers are moving in the same direction. Seagate’s fiscal 2026 revenue increased 34% to $12.2 billion, while fourth-quarter revenue climbed 48% to $3.63 billion. Adjusted gross margin jumped to 52.7%, and adjusted EPS more than doubled to $5.71. Management expects first-quarter revenue of roughly $4.1 billion, implying growth of about 56% from a year earlier.

For Sparks, that combination matters because a significant portion of the expected growth is backed by customer commitments already in place. Seagate trades at around 15 times expected fiscal 2028 earnings, putting it at a similar valuation to Western Digital.

Sandisk has taken a different approach to securing its future business. The company has agreements with eight customers covering a substantial portion of its upcoming production. More than half of its fiscal 2027 volumes and roughly two-thirds of fiscal 2028’s volumes are expected to fall under those contracts.

There is another important feature. The agreements include minimum pricing provisions, meaning Sandisk has some protection if memory prices weaken. Management says the contracts would represent at least $93.9 billion of revenue even at those contractual floor prices.

Sparks considers that a significant advantage, but there is still an unanswered question. Those pricing protections have yet to be put through a serious memory market downturn, so investors don’t know how they will perform when industry conditions become less favorable.

Sandisk is coming off an exceptional year, with fiscal 2026 revenue soaring 175% to $20.25 billion as memory prices rose and data center demand strengthened. That growth gives the company plenty of appeal, but Sparks remains cautious about assuming current conditions will last indefinitely.

So, down to business, which stock does Sparks think represents the best opportunity right now?

“My pick is Seagate. Its contracts already fix pricing for all of calendar 2027, and most of its nearline capacity is spoken for into the year after that. Growth is accelerating, too,” the 5-star analyst said.

As for the other two, Western Digital offers a similar valuation and is benefiting from the same strong demand environment. However, Sparks isn’t convinced that enough of its production is secured beyond 2026 to give him the same confidence as Seagate. Sandisk arguably has the most downside protection of the three thanks to its pricing floors, but those safeguards have yet to face a real industry downturn. Sparks would prefer to see how they hold up before taking a more bullish stance. (To watch Sparks’ track record, click here)

With a large installed base already paying for cloud storage, higher AI limits could strengthen Services revenue.

Despite these positives, Fontes remains bearish on Apple stock because of its valuation. Even assuming 10% annual revenue growth through fiscal 2032 and gradual margin expansion, he estimates an annual total return of about 7.1%. Under more conservative, cyclical growth assumptions, that falls closer to 6.3%. In other words, Fontes believes Apple’s expected return is not high enough to compensate investors for the risks. With the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield around 4.9% and the S&P 500’s historical return around 10%, Fontes believes Apple does not currently offer a sufficient margin of safety.
